Population Dynamics and Matrix Equations

We are going to start today by doing a quick review of the two-kingdom population model from our recent quiz. The movie Frozen has a special place in my heart because it is the movie we watched all the time when we were locked down, so we will use the kingdoms of Arendelle and Weaselton for our setup.

Previously, we modeled zombies and humans on an hourly basis. Now, we are simulating population migration on a yearly basis. Suppose that every year, 5\% of the population moves from Arendelle to Weaselton, and 15\% moves from Weaselton to Arendelle.

We want to write a system of two equations that captures this scenario. Let a_n be the population of Arendelle at year n, and w_n be the population of Weaselton at year n. These populations depend on the populations from the year prior, a_{n-1} and w_{n-1}.

If Arendelle loses 5\% of its people every year, that means 100\% - 5\% = 95\% of the people are staying. At the same time, Arendelle gains 15\% of Weaselton’s population from the prior year. We can write this as: \begin{equation} a_n = 0.95 a_{n-1} + 0.15 w_{n-1} \tag{1} \end{equation}

Similarly, Weaselton loses 15\% of its people, meaning 85\% stay. It also gains the 5\% that left Arendelle. This gives us our second equation: \begin{equation} w_n = 0.05 a_{n-1} + 0.85 w_{n-1} \tag{2} \end{equation}

We can rearrange this system of equations into a single matrix equation. We extract the coefficients into a 2 \times 2 matrix and multiply it by a 2D vector representing the prior year’s population: \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} a_n \\ w_n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.95 & 0.15 \\ 0.05 & 0.85 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a_{n-1} \\ w_{n-1} \end{pmatrix} \tag{3} \end{equation}

If you multiply this matrix by the vector, you recover the exact system of equations we started with.

Over time, as we multiply our population vector by this matrix year after year, the vector points in a new direction, but eventually, it settles.

If we assume the total population between the two kingdoms is 1 million people, we can determine the final distribution. Because the rate of people moving from Weaselton to Arendelle (15\%) is three times larger than the rate moving the other way (5\%), Arendelle will end up with three times as many people as Weaselton.

At equilibrium, Arendelle will have 750,000 people, and Weaselton will have 250,000 people.

One unrealistic assumption about this model is that there are no births or deaths; we are assuming the total population stays exactly the same year after year. While it is a gross oversimplification, it is an excellent tool for learning linear algebra.

Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Math of Equilibrium

I just gave you the answer for the final population, but how do we know for sure that there will be three times more people in Arendelle at equilibrium?

The linear algebra buzzword for equilibrium is eigenvector. The word “eigen” comes from German, meaning “proper” or “characteristic.” In our context, the eigenvector represents the equilibrium population distribution or ratio.

Before we can find the eigenvector, we first have to find the eigenvalues, denoted by the Greek letter \lambda (lambda). Each eigenvalue has its own corresponding eigenvector.

The fundamental eigenvalue equation states that multiplying our matrix by the eigenvector is the same as multiplying that eigenvector by the scalar eigenvalue \lambda: \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} 0.95 & 0.15 \\ 0.05 & 0.85 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a \\ w \end{pmatrix} = \lambda \begin{pmatrix} a \\ w \end{pmatrix} \tag{4} \end{equation}

To find the eigenvalues for our 2 \times 2 matrix, we set up a determinant. We take our original matrix, subtract \lambda from each of the diagonal elements, and set the determinant of this new matrix equal to zero: \begin{equation} \det(A - \lambda I) = \begin{vmatrix} 0.95 - \lambda & 0.15 \\ 0.05 & 0.85 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0 \tag{5} \end{equation}

To evaluate a 2 \times 2 determinant, we cross-multiply the diagonals and subtract the products: \begin{equation} (0.95 - \lambda)(0.85 - \lambda) - (0.05)(0.15) = 0 \tag{6} \end{equation}

If we expand this out and do the arithmetic, we get a quadratic equation: \begin{equation} \lambda^2 - 1.8\lambda + 0.8 = 0 \tag{7} \end{equation}

Factoring this quadratic equation gives us: \begin{equation} (\lambda - 1)(\lambda - 0.8) = 0 \tag{8} \end{equation}

This means we have two possible eigenvalues: \lambda = 1 and \lambda = 0.8. Because we know our total population is conserved (nobody is dying, no new babies are being born), \lambda = 1 is the physically sensible eigenvalue that represents conserved population.

Now we need to find the eigenvector corresponding to \lambda = 1. We return to our matrix equation, but instead of looking at year n and year n-1, we assume the population has settled. We set the matrix multiplied by our vector equal to \lambda times that same vector: \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} 0.95 & 0.15 \\ 0.05 & 0.85 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a \\ w \end{pmatrix} = 1 \begin{pmatrix} a \\ w \end{pmatrix} \tag{9} \end{equation}

Converting the top row back into an algebraic equation: \begin{equation} 0.95a + 0.15w = 1a \tag{10} \end{equation}

Subtracting 0.95a from both sides gives: \begin{equation} 0.15w = 0.05a \tag{11} \end{equation}

Dividing both sides by 0.05, we find: \begin{equation} 3w = a \tag{12} \end{equation}

This confirms mathematically what we reasoned earlier: Arendelle’s population (a) is always three times Weaselton’s population (w). The eigenvector is \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}. Given a total population of 1 million, this scales to 750,000 for Arendelle and 250,000 for Weaselton.

What about the other eigenvalue, \lambda = 0.8? If you run through the same math, you get an eigenvector of \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}. This suggests that one kingdom has a negative population. That is malarkey—you cannot have a negative population. Therefore, this eigenvalue is physically non-applicable for this specific scenario.

If we were modeling a different scenario and found an eigenvector of (2, -1), what would that physically mean, and why would we reject it?

An eigenvector of (2, -1) implies that one of the kingdoms has a negative number of people living in it. Since a negative population is physically impossible, we reject the eigenvalue associated with this eigenvector as non-applicable to our real-world scenario.

Expanding the Model: Three Kingdoms

Things get more interesting when we handle a more complex scenario. Let’s add a third kingdom. We will call it Monaco, denoted by m_n.

Suppose we have the following migration rates every year:

  • Leaving Arendelle: 5\% move to Weaselton, 8\% move to Monaco. Total leaving = 13\%. Therefore, 87\% stay.

  • Leaving Weaselton: 15\% move to Arendelle, 6\% move to Monaco. Total leaving = 21\%. Therefore, 79\% stay.

  • Leaving Monaco: 12\% move to Arendelle, 3\% move to Weaselton. Total leaving = 15\%. Therefore, 85\% stay.

We can write next year’s population for each kingdom based on the people who stay plus the people who arrive: \begin{align} a_n &= 0.87 a_{n-1} + 0.15 w_{n-1} + 0.12 m_{n-1} \tag{13}\\ w_n &= 0.05 a_{n-1} + 0.79 w_{n-1} + 0.03 m_{n-1} \tag{14}\\ m_n &= 0.08 a_{n-1} + 0.06 w_{n-1} + 0.85 m_{n-1} \tag{15} \end{align}

We can package this into a 3 \times 3 matrix equation: \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} 0.87 & 0.15 & 0.12 \\ 0.05 & 0.79 & 0.03 \\ 0.08 & 0.06 & 0.85 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a_{n-1} \\ w_{n-1} \\ m_{n-1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a_n \\ w_n \\ m_n \end{pmatrix} \tag{16} \end{equation}

Notice the structure of this matrix. The diagonal elements (0.87, 0.79, 0.85) represent the fraction of people staying in their respective kingdoms. We can think of these as self terms. Everything else—the off-diagonal elements—represents people moving between kingdoms, which we can call interaction terms.

As a quick check, notice that each column adds up exactly to 1 (e.g., 0.87 + 0.05 + 0.08 = 1.00). This happens because everyone in a kingdom either stays or moves; no one is born or dies, so the fractions leaving a kingdom must add to 100\%. The total population is conserved.

If a new disease caused a 2\% mortality rate in Arendelle each year, what would the first column of our matrix add up to instead of 1.00?

The first column would add up to 0.98. Because 2\% of the population is removed from the system, only 98\% of Arendelle’s population is conserved to either stay or move to another kingdom.

To find the equilibrium state, we set up the eigenvalue equation. Because equilibrium means the populations have settled and are no longer changing from year to year, we drop the n and n-1 subscripts. The vector is the same on both sides of the equation, multiplied by our eigenvalue \lambda: \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} 0.87 & 0.15 & 0.12 \\ 0.05 & 0.79 & 0.03 \\ 0.08 & 0.06 & 0.85 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a \\ w \\ m \end{pmatrix} = \lambda \begin{pmatrix} a \\ w \\ m \end{pmatrix} \tag{17} \end{equation}

Computational Eigen Solvers

Finding the eigenvalues for a 2 \times 2 matrix by hand was manageable, requiring us to solve a quadratic equation. However, doing this for a 3 \times 3 matrix requires solving a cubic polynomial, which is tedious.

This is what computers are for. Computers love eating eigenvalue equations for lunch. If you feed a matrix into a Python script, it will reward you by spitting out the proper eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

Below are two Python scripts using the numpy library. The first is a 2D solver, and the second is a 3D solver. I have already plugged in the migration matrices for our specific kingdom problems into these scripts.

2D Eigen Solver

Show Python code
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
"""

2D eigen solver

"""

import numpy as np

# Define a 2x2 matrix for Arendelle and Weaselton
A = np.array([[0.95, 0.15],
              [0.05, 0.85]])

# Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(A)

# Display results
print("Eigenvalues:")
print(eigenvalues)
print("\nEigenvectors:")
print(eigenvectors)

When we run this script, the solver outputs eigenvalues of 1 and 0.8. The eigenvector columns are approximately (0.949, 0.316) and (-0.707, 0.707). Looking at the physically sensible eigenvalue of 1, the ratio of 0.949 to 0.316 is exactly 3:1, which matches the hand-calculated vector of \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}.

3D Eigen Solver

Show Python code
"""

3D eigen solver

"""

import numpy as np

# Define a 3x3 matrix for Arendelle, Weaselton, and Monaco
A = np.array([[0.87, 0.15, 0.12],
              [0.05, 0.79, 0.03],
              [0.08, 0.06, 0.85]])

# Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(A)

# Display results
print("Eigenvalues:")
print(eigenvalues)
print("\nEigenvectors:")
print(eigenvectors)

When we run this script, it prints eigenvalues of 1, 0.73, and 0.78.

The eigenvector column corresponding to the sensible eigenvalue (\lambda = 1) is (-0.802, -0.267, -0.535). Because all the entries are negative, we can simply multiply the entire vector by -1 to get positive populations. The ratio of these numbers is roughly 3 : 1 : 2.

Why are we mathematically allowed to multiply the eigenvector by -1? Doesn’t that change the answer?

An eigenvector defines a ratio or a direction, not a fixed set of absolute values. Multiplying the entire vector by a constant like -1 just scales it, but the relative proportions between the kingdoms remain exactly the same. Since we eventually scale the ratios to match our total population of 1 million anyway, flipping the signs is a valid and necessary step.

If we divide each entry by the sum of the entries and multiply by our total population of 1 million, we find the final equilibrium populations:

  • Arendelle (a): 500,000

  • Weaselton (w): 166,667

  • Monaco (m): 333,333

Arendelle ends up being the biggest kingdom. This makes physical sense based on our rates: Arendelle gains the most from both other kingdoms and loses the least.

Three Kingdoms and the Eigen Solver Worksheet

Below are the blank and filled-out images of the worksheet from class, followed by a text transcription of the completed key.

1. A third kingdom

Quiz 08 had two kingdoms. Now a third kingdom joins. The arrows show what fraction of each kingdom moves each year.

  • Arendelle moves 5\% to Weaselton and 8\% to Monaco.

  • Weaselton moves 15\% to Arendelle and 6\% to Monaco.

  • Monaco moves 12\% to Arendelle and 3\% to Weaselton.

Add up the rates leaving each kingdom:

  • Arendelle: 13\%, so 87\% stay.

  • Weaselton: 21\%, so 79\% stay.

  • Monaco: 15\%, so 85\% stay.

2. Three equations

Let a, w, m be the populations of Arendelle, Weaselton, and Monaco. Write next year’s population of each kingdom from this year’s (people who stay + people who arrive): \begin{align*} a_n &= 0.87 a_{n-1} + 0.15 w_{n-1} + 0.12 m_{n-1} \\ w_n &= 0.05 a_{n-1} + 0.79 w_{n-1} + 0.03 m_{n-1} \\ m_n &= 0.08 a_{n-1} + 0.06 w_{n-1} + 0.85 m_{n-1} \end{align*}

3. The 3 \times 3 matrix equation

Put the same numbers in a matrix. Rows: who you move to. Columns: who you move from.
Year by year (year n-1 to year n): \begin{equation*} \begin{pmatrix} 0.87 & 0.15 & 0.12 \\ 0.05 & 0.79 & 0.03 \\ 0.08 & 0.06 & 0.85 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a_{n-1} \\ w_{n-1} \\ m_{n-1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a_n \\ w_n \\ m_n \end{pmatrix} \end{equation*}

After a long time (the eigenvalue equation; write the symbol for the eigenvalue in the box): \begin{equation*} \begin{pmatrix} 0.87 & 0.15 & 0.12 \\ 0.05 & 0.79 & 0.03 \\ 0.08 & 0.06 & 0.85 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a \\ w \\ m \end{pmatrix} = \lambda \begin{pmatrix} a \\ w \\ m \end{pmatrix} \end{equation*}

Each column of your matrix adds up to 1. Why?
Everyone in a kingdom either stays or moves; no one is born or dies, so the fractions leaving a kingdom (its column) add to 100\%. The total population is conserved.

Why did we drop the subscripts n and n-1 in the eigenvalue equation?
After a long time, the populations settle. Year n-1 and year n are the same vector, so we just call it (a, w, m). “Eigen” means equilibrium—there is no change after a step because we have settled.

4. Get the eigen solver

Physically sensible eigenvalue = 1 (the total population stays the same), and every entry of its eigenvector has the same sign (if all are negative, multiply by -1). Mixed signs would mean a negative population.

5. Test the solver on the 2 \times 2 from Quiz 08

Type in the matrix we solved by hand: \begin{equation*} A = \begin{pmatrix} 0.95 & 0.15 \\ 0.05 & 0.85 \end{pmatrix} \end{equation*} Eigenvalues: 1 and 0.8.
Eigenvector columns: (0.949, 0.316) and (-0.707, 0.707).
Physically sensible eigenvalue: 1. Ratio a:w = 3:1. Matches c(3, 1) by hand? Yes.
For 1 million people: a = 750,000, w = 250,000.

6. Now the 3 \times 3

Type your matrix from Section 3 into the 3D solver.
Eigenvalues: 1, 0.73, 0.78.
Eigenvector column for the sensible one: (-0.802, -0.267, -0.535).
Divide each entry by their sum, then multiply by 1 million (the total population):
a = 500,000, w = 166,667, m = 333,333.
Which kingdom ends up biggest? Does that match your rates?
Arendelle (3:1:2). Arendelle gains the most from both other kingdoms and loses the least.

Computing Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors for a 3 \times 3 Matrix

While we rely on computers to solve 3 \times 3 matrices, it is helpful to understand the underlying math that the computer is executing. The process is a direct extension of what we did by hand for the 2 \times 2 matrix.

We start with the eigenvalue equation: \begin{equation} A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v} \tag{18} \end{equation} where A is our 3 \times 3 matrix, \mathbf{v} is the eigenvector, and \lambda is the eigenvalue.

We can rearrange this equation by subtracting \lambda\mathbf{v} from both sides. To factor out the vector \mathbf{v}, we must multiply \lambda by the 3 \times 3 identity matrix I: \begin{equation} (A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = 0 \tag{19} \end{equation}

For this equation to have a non-trivial solution (meaning \mathbf{v} is not just a vector of all zeros), the determinant of the matrix (A - \lambda I) must be exactly zero: \begin{equation} \det(A - \lambda I) = 0 \tag{20} \end{equation}

For a 3 \times 3 matrix, setting up this determinant looks like this: \begin{equation} \det \begin{vmatrix} A_{11} - \lambda & A_{12} & A_{13} \\ A_{21} & A_{22} - \lambda & A_{23} \\ A_{31} & A_{32} & A_{33} - \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0 \tag{21} \end{equation}

When you expand this determinant, instead of getting a quadratic equation like we did for the 2 \times 2 matrix, you generate a cubic polynomial in terms of \lambda: \begin{equation} -\lambda^3 + c_2\lambda^2 + c_1\lambda + c_0 = 0 \tag{22} \end{equation} where c_2, c_1, and c_0 are constants derived from the elements of matrix A.

Solving a cubic equation by hand to find the three roots (\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3) is highly tedious. Once the three eigenvalues are found, you must substitute each one back into the equation (A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = 0 and solve the resulting system of three linear equations to find the corresponding eigenvector \mathbf{v} for each \lambda.

Because finding the roots of a cubic polynomial and solving 3 \times 3 linear systems by hand is prone to arithmetic errors and takes a long time, we use computational solvers to handle the heavy lifting.
